lead: A generating function turns a whole sequence into one power series, so adding, shifting and multiplying sequences become algebra on power series, done the way you handle polynomials. It exists because counting and recurrences often produce sequences that are hard to compare term by term. Packed as one object, they can be simplified and read back. You use it for binomial identities, recurrence solving, and counting arrangements.
prereq: You need: combinations and the binomial series from 3.2, and basic algebra from Unit 2.

sections.h3: Pack a sequence into a series

blocks.text: A sequence a₀, a₁, a₂, … can be stored as one power series. The ordinary generating function (OGF) of the sequence is G(x) = Σ_{n≥0} a_n xⁿ. The symbol x is a placeholder, not a number to substitute. a_n is the nth term; for example a₀ is the first term. The coefficient of xⁿ in G(x) is written [xⁿ]G(x), and it equals a_n. No value of x is needed to define the series.

This is formal algebra. Two series are equal when every coefficient matches; we add and multiply them like polynomials, ignoring convergence. That freedom is the point: an infinite list becomes one algebraic object. Some syllabi call this simply the generating function. For example, the sequence 1, 2, 3, … has G(x)=1+2x+3x²+⋯.

blocks.where: a_n is the term at index n; x is a formal variable.

blocks.text: Three series cover most exam problems. As numeric identities, 1/(1−x) = Σxⁿ needs |x| < 1, and 1/(1−ax) = Σaⁿxⁿ needs |ax| < 1. The binomial series (1+x)ⁿ = Σ C(n,k)x^k is a finite sum, so it always holds. As formal power series, none of them needs any condition on x. C(n,k) is the binomial coefficient from 3.2.

blocks.where: a is a constant; C(n,k) counts k-subsets of an n-set; n is a non-negative integer.

items: Shifting: x^k G(x) has coefficients 0 up to k−1, then a₀, a₁, … at positions k, k+1, ….
Scaling: G(ax) has coefficients a_n aⁿ.
Convolution: if H(x)=G(x)F(x), then h_n=Σ_{k=0}^{n} a_k b_{n−k}.

blocks.text: Convolution is why generating functions solve counting problems: choosing k items from one part and n−k from another adds over all k. In the convolution formula, F(x) = Σ_{k≥0} b_k x^k, so b_k is the coefficient of x^k in F(x), and a_k = [x^k]G(x).

A rational generating function can be split by partial fractions into pieces from the known list. First divide P by Q if deg P ≥ deg Q, and keep only the remainder over Q; also Q must have Q(0) ≠ 0 so that every factor can be written as (1−αx); if not, take out a power of x first. To find [xⁿ] P(x)/Q(x), factor Q(x), write the fraction as A/(1−αx)+B/(1−βx)+⋯, then read coefficients: [xⁿ] 1/(1−αx)=αⁿ. For a repeated factor (1−αx)², use 1/(1−αx)²=Σ(n+1)αⁿxⁿ.

If Q(x) has (1−αx)^m, include terms A₁/(1−αx)+⋯+A_m/(1−αx)^m. The worked example below carries this out for the odd numbers. The same method will solve recurrences in 3.7, where you first find G(x) from the recurrence, then extract coefficients.

figure.caption: The odd-number sequence becomes a power series, splits into two known series, and closes into one rational function. Notice that the final coefficient of xⁿ is still 2n+1.

spec.title: From sequence to closed form
spec.aria: The odd-number sequence is written as a power series, split into two known series, and closed to (1 plus x) over (1 minus x) squared.

examples.question: Find the ordinary generating function of the sequence 1, 3, 5, 7, … where a_n = 2n+1 for n ≥ 0. Write it in closed form using known series, and verify the coefficients of x⁰, x¹, x², x³.
steps: Start with G(x)=Σ_{n≥0}(2n+1)xⁿ. Split the sum: G(x)=2Σ_{n≥0}n xⁿ + Σ_{n≥0}xⁿ.
Use the known series Σ_{n≥0}n xⁿ=x/(1−x)².
Put over the common denominator (1−x)²: G(x)=[2x+(1−x)]/(1−x)²=(1+x)/(1−x)².
Check coefficients from 1/(1−x)²=Σ(n+1)xⁿ. Multiplying by 1+x gives coefficient of xⁿ as (n+1)+n=2n+1.
For n=0,1,2,3 the coefficients are 1, 3, 5, 7, matching the sequence.
examples.answer: The ordinary generating function is G(x)=(1+x)/(1−x)², and its coefficient of xⁿ is 2n+1; the first four coefficients are 1, 3, 5, 7.

traps: Treating x as a number and checking convergence. For formal power series, only the coefficients matter; no convergence test is needed.
Confusing the index with the value: the coefficient of x⁵ is a₅, not 5. Write [xⁿ]G(x)=a_n to keep the two separate.
Forgetting the constant term: 1/(1−x) starts at 1, while x/(1−x)² starts at x. A missing a₀ shifts every answer.
Sign slips in partial fractions, especially with repeated factors such as (1−x)². Substitute x=1 and x=1/2 back into the cover-up equations to check.

quiz.q: Define the ordinary generating function of a sequence a₀, a₁, a₂, ….
quiz.a: G(x)=Σ_{n≥0}a_n xⁿ. The coefficient of xⁿ is a_n, and x is a formal variable.

quiz.q: Why can two generating functions be multiplied without checking convergence?
quiz.a: They are formal power series. Multiplication is defined coefficient by coefficient: the coefficient of xⁿ in the product is Σ_{k=0}^n a_k b_{n−k}. No numeric value of x is used.

quiz.q: Find the ordinary generating function of 2, 4, 6, 8, … .
Find the coefficient of x⁴ in (1+x)/(1−x)².
quiz.a: From the worked example, the coefficient of xⁿ is 2n+1. Put n=4: 2·4+1=9.

quiz.q: Explain how the product 1/(1−x) · 1/(1−x) gives the sequence 1, 2, 3, … .
quiz.a: Each factor has coefficients all equal to 1. Convolution gives h_n=Σ_{k=0}^n 1·1=n+1. So 1/(1−x)²=Σ(n+1)xⁿ.

beyond: Not for the exam. Generating functions are the backbone of analytic combinatorics, where singularity analysis gives asymptotic growth of sequences. In computer science they appear in the analysis of algorithms, hashing, and formal languages. Search 'ordinary generating function', 'coefficient extraction', and 'analytic combinatorics' to go further.
